subject: Ch3: Grammars & Syntax Analysis (Hard)
description: Hard-level MCQs on context-free grammars, derivations, parse trees, ambiguity, precedence/associativity, grammar transformations (left recursion, left factoring, useless/unit/ε removal), and the Chomsky hierarchy.

questions.text: For an unambiguous grammar, the number of distinct leftmost derivations of a given sentence is:
options: Always zero, because leftmost derivations are undefined for unambiguous grammars
Exactly one
Equal to the number of nonterminals appearing anywhere in the entire grammar
Possibly many, since each different parse tree contributes its own leftmost derivation
questions.shortExplanation: Unambiguous ⇒ exactly one leftmost derivation per sentence.
questions.explanation: Unambiguity means each sentence has a unique parse tree, equivalently a unique leftmost (and unique rightmost) derivation.

questions.text: The grammar E → E + E | E * E | (E) | id is ambiguous primarily because it fails to encode:
options: Operator precedence and associativity
The finite set of terminal symbols that the language is allowed to use
A designated start symbol from which all derivations must begin
Any productions that allow the nonterminal id to be expanded into tokens
questions.shortExplanation: No precedence/associativity → multiple parse trees.
questions.explanation: Without structural encoding of precedence and associativity, expressions like id+id*id have more than one parse tree, making the grammar ambiguous.

questions.text: Eliminating left recursion from A → A a | A b | c | d yields:
options: A → (c | d) A',  A' → (a | b) A' | ε, which is the standard right-recursive replacement scheme
A → a A' | b A',  A' → c | d, swapping which symbols become the prefixes and the tails
A → c | d only, discarding the recursive alternatives a and b entirely from the grammar
A → A a | A b unchanged, since these alternatives are not actually left-recursive at all
questions.shortExplanation: Group non-recursive alternatives as prefixes; recurse on the tails.
questions.explanation: With α-set {a,b} and β-set {c,d}, the standard rule gives A → c A' | d A' and A' → a A' | b A' | ε, written compactly as in option B.

questions.text: Which transformation removes the need for backtracking by isolating a shared prefix?
options: Left recursion elimination, which reorganizes recursive alternatives so top-down parsing terminates
Unit production removal, which copies a nonterminal's right-hand sides into the referring rule
ε-production removal, which adds variants that omit each nullable nonterminal from a body
Left factoring
questions.shortExplanation: Left factoring defers the decision past a common prefix.
questions.explanation: Left factoring rewrites A → αβ₁ | αβ₂ as A → αA', A' → β₁ | β₂, so a predictive parser can postpone its choice and avoid backtracking.

questions.text: In removing useless symbols, the CORRECT order is to first remove:
options: All terminals first, and then carefully prune the nonterminals that depend upon them
ε-productions first, and then proceed to eliminate every remaining unit production
Unreachable symbols first, and only afterwards remove the non-generating symbols from the grammar
Non-generating (non-productive) symbols that derive no terminal string, and only afterwards the unreachable symbols that the start symbol can never reach
questions.shortExplanation: Remove non-generating first, then unreachable.
questions.explanation: Doing it in the other order can leave useless symbols; one must first delete symbols that derive no terminal string, then remove what becomes unreachable.

questions.text: A right-sentential form is any sentential form that appears in some:
options: Rightmost derivation, in which the rightmost nonterminal of the current form is expanded
Leftmost derivation, in which the leftmost nonterminal is always the one expanded next
Parse-tree traversal performed strictly in left-to-right post-order across the leaves
Regular expression that has been compiled into an equivalent finite-state automaton
questions.shortExplanation: Right-sentential forms arise in rightmost derivations.
questions.explanation: By definition a right-sentential form is a sentential form occurring in a rightmost derivation; it is central to LR parsing and handles.

questions.text: Which statement about inherently ambiguous context-free languages is TRUE?
options: Every context-free language can be generated by at least one suitably constructed unambiguous grammar
Every regular language is inherently ambiguous and admits no deterministic recognizer
Ambiguity in any grammar can always be removed by repeatedly applying left factoring
Some context-free languages admit only ambiguous grammars, never any unambiguous grammar
questions.shortExplanation: Inherently ambiguous CFLs admit no unambiguous grammar.
questions.explanation: There exist context-free languages for which every generating grammar is ambiguous; such languages are called inherently ambiguous.

questions.text: To make + right-associative in E, the grammar should be written as:
options: E → T + E | T
E → E + T | T, which is the standard form used to make the operator left-associative
E → T + T, which permits only a single addition and so encodes no associativity at all
E → E + E | T, which is ambiguous and therefore fixes no particular associativity
questions.shortExplanation: Right recursion (T + E) gives right associativity.
questions.explanation: Right-recursive productions (operator's right operand is the recursive nonterminal) yield right associativity; left recursion yields left associativity.

questions.text: The yield of a parse tree together with the tree's shape determines the:
options: Token stream only, ignoring entirely how the tokens are grouped into subexpressions
Final target machine code emitted after register allocation and instruction selection
FIRST set of the start symbol, computed from the leading terminals of its productions
Syntactic structure, the grouping of the sentence into its nested subexpression part
questions.shortExplanation: Tree shape encodes grouping/structure; yield is the sentence.
questions.explanation: The leaves (yield) give the sentence, while the internal structure shows how subexpressions group — the syntactic structure the parser must recover.

questions.text: Removing ε-productions from a grammar may require:
options: Adding new productions that omit each nullable nonterminal in all possible combinations, so the language is preserved even after the ε-rules themselves are deleted
Converting the entire grammar into an equivalent right-linear regular grammar first
Deliberately introducing left recursion into every production that was previously nullable
Deleting the start symbol and replacing it with the first nonterminal that derives a terminal
questions.shortExplanation: Account for nullable nonterminals by adding omitting variants.
questions.explanation: For each production containing nullable nonterminals, you add variants with those nonterminals removed (in all subsets), preserving the language (minus ε if needed).

questions.text: In the Chomsky hierarchy, the class recognized by a (nondeterministic) pushdown automaton is:
options: Regular (Type 3), the same class accepted by ordinary finite automata without any stack
Recursively enumerable (Type 0), the class accepted by general unrestricted Turing machines
Context-free (Type 2)
Context-sensitive (Type 1), the class accepted by linear-bounded Turing machines
questions.shortExplanation: NPDA ↔ context-free languages.
questions.explanation: Nondeterministic pushdown automata recognize exactly the context-free languages, Type 2 in the Chomsky hierarchy.

questions.text: Which is a unit production?
options: A → ε, an epsilon production whose right-hand side is the empty string of symbols
A → B C, whose right-hand side consists of exactly two nonterminals placed in sequence
A → B
A → a B, whose right-hand side mixes one terminal together with a single nonterminal
questions.shortExplanation: A single nonterminal RHS is a unit production.
questions.explanation: A unit (single) production has exactly one nonterminal on its right side, e.g. A → B; these are often removed to simplify grammars.

questions.text: The context-free languages are NOT closed under:
options: Kleene star, the operation forming all finite repetitions of strings from a CFL
Intersection
Union, the operation that combines the strings of two given context-free languages
Concatenation, which appends every string of one CFL to every string of another
questions.shortExplanation: CFLs are not closed under intersection.
questions.explanation: CFLs are closed under union, concatenation, and star, but not under intersection (e.g., aⁿbⁿcⁿ is the intersection of two CFLs).

questions.text: A grammar with the production set { S → S S | a } generates strings of a's and is ambiguous because:
options: 'aaa' has more than one parse tree, arising from the two different ways the production S S can associate the leftmost and rightmost copies of S
It cannot derive the single-symbol string 'a' through any valid sequence of productions
It is purely left-recursive, and left recursion by itself always forces ambiguity here
It has no terminal symbols at all, so no terminal string can ever actually be produced
questions.shortExplanation: Different associations of S S give multiple trees.
questions.explanation: S → S S can group a string of a's in several ways (like unparenthesized association), so a string such as 'aaa' has multiple parse trees.

questions.text: Leftmost and rightmost derivations of the same sentence in an unambiguous grammar:
options: Yield two different terminal sentences even though they start from the same start symbol
Always apply the productions in exactly the same order at every single derivation step
Correspond to exactly the same unique parse tree, but may apply the very same productions in a different relative order during the derivation
Cannot both exist, because any grammar admits only one of the two derivation styles
questions.shortExplanation: Same tree, different replacement order.
questions.explanation: Both derivations describe the unique parse tree; they differ only in the order nonterminals are expanded (leftmost vs rightmost).

questions.text: Which grammar is NOT context-free (violates the CFG form)?
options: A B → B A, a rule with two symbols on its left-hand side, beyond plain context-free format
S → a S b | ε, a perfectly valid context-free rule with a single nonterminal on its left
E → E + T | T, a left-recursive but entirely legitimate context-free expression grammar
S → A B,  A → a,  B → b, a standard context-free grammar with single-nonterminal left sides
questions.shortExplanation: CFG left sides must be a single nonterminal.
questions.explanation: A production must have exactly one nonterminal on the left; 'A B → B A' has a multi-symbol left side, making it context-sensitive, not context-free.

questions.text: The dangling-else ambiguity is conventionally resolved by the rule that an else matches the:
options: Outermost unmatched if, that is, the very first enclosing if that still lacks an else
Nearest (closest) unmatched if, the closest preceding if that still lacks any else
Last statement of the enclosing block, regardless of whether it happens to be an if
First if textually appearing anywhere earlier in the program's source code stream
questions.shortExplanation: Else binds to the nearest unmatched if.
questions.explanation: Most languages adopt the 'closest if' rule, enforced by a grammar distinguishing matched and unmatched statements.

questions.text: If L1 is context-free and L2 is regular, then L1 ∩ L2 is:
options: Undecidable, in the sense that no algorithm can determine the membership of the result
Always regular, because intersecting with a regular language must collapse it to regular
Always context-free, since a CFL intersected with a regular language stays context-free
Never context-free, since intersection always pushes a language beyond the context-free class
questions.shortExplanation: CFL ∩ regular is context-free.
questions.explanation: Although CFLs are not closed under intersection in general, the intersection of a context-free language with a regular language is always context-free.

questions.text: A non-immediate (indirect) left recursion such as A → B a, B → A c | d requires:
options: No special handling whatsoever for top-down parsing, since only direct recursion causes loops
Substituting B's bodies into A first, then eliminating the now-immediate left recursion seen
Applying left factoring only, since a shared common prefix is the sole underlying problem
Removing the start symbol and choosing a fresh start symbol that avoids the recursion
questions.shortExplanation: Substitute to expose immediate recursion, then eliminate.
questions.explanation: Indirect left recursion is handled by ordering nonterminals and substituting earlier ones (B into A) so the recursion becomes immediate and removable.

questions.text: The set of all sentential forms of a grammar:
options: Equals exactly the language generated by the grammar, with no additional strings included
Contains only fully terminal strings, the same as the language the grammar generates
Includes intermediate strings that still contain nonterminals, so it is in general a proper superset of the terminal-only language the grammar generates
Is always a finite set, regardless of whether the grammar is recursive or not recursive
questions.shortExplanation: Sentential forms may contain nonterminals; language is terminal-only.
questions.explanation: The language is the set of terminal-only sentential forms; the full set of sentential forms also contains intermediate strings with nonterminals.

questions.text: Which property must hold for a grammar to be suitable for top-down predictive parsing?
options: It must contain ε-productions in order for the predictive parser to terminate correctly
It must be free of left recursion and, usually, left-factored for deterministic LL choice
It must be ambiguous so that the predictive parser can freely choose among parse trees
It must be right-linear, restricting every recursive call to a single trailing nonterminal
questions.shortExplanation: No left recursion; left-factored.
questions.explanation: Top-down predictive parsing needs the grammar to avoid left recursion (to prevent infinite loops) and be left-factored to allow deterministic choice.

questions.text: Two grammars are equivalent if they:
options: Use the same name for their start symbol, even if their productions happen to differ
Have exactly the same set of productions, written symbol-for-symbol in the same notation
Generate exactly the same language, the same set of all terminal strings despite rules
Have the same total number of distinct nonterminals appearing across all productions
questions.shortExplanation: Equivalence = same generated language.
questions.explanation: Grammar equivalence is defined purely by the language generated, regardless of the productions or symbol names used.

questions.text: A cycle in a grammar (A ⇒+ A) is undesirable because it:
options: Automatically makes the grammar regular and thus recognizable by a finite automaton
Removes left recursion as a convenient side effect of the repeated self-derivation
Adds a useful kind of ambiguity that helps the parser disambiguate competing parse trees
Permits arbitrarily long derivations that produce no new terminal symbols at all, needlessly complicating parsing and termination analysis
questions.shortExplanation: Cycles allow infinite derivation steps with no progress.
questions.explanation: Cycles let a nonterminal derive itself, creating unbounded derivations that yield no terminals, which must be eliminated for well-behaved parsing.

questions.text: Encoding precedence so that * binds tighter than + is typically done by:
options: Putting both + and * inside one single production so they are treated at the same level
Introducing separate nonterminals (E for +, T for *, F for atoms) on different stratified levels, so the higher-precedence operator sits deeper in the parse tree
Deliberately making the grammar ambiguous so the parser may pick either grouping freely
Removing all parentheses from the grammar so that no explicit grouping is ever possible
questions.shortExplanation: Stratify with E/T/F levels for precedence.
questions.explanation: Layering nonterminals (E → E + T, T → T * F, F → (E) | id) places higher-precedence operators deeper in the tree, enforcing precedence unambiguously.

questions.text: Which statement about parse trees and derivations is FALSE?
options: Every single leftmost derivation corresponds to several distinct parse trees at once
An ambiguous grammar can produce two distinct parse trees for a single input sentence
Every parse tree corresponds to one and only one leftmost derivation of the sentence
A parse tree abstracts away the particular order in which the derivation steps were taken
questions.shortExplanation: A leftmost derivation maps to exactly one parse tree.
questions.explanation: Statement D is false: a given leftmost derivation determines a single parse tree; it is ambiguity that allows multiple trees for one sentence.

questions.text: The language { aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1 } is context-free but not regular; a grammar for it is:
options: S → S a b, which is left-recursive with no base case and therefore derives no terminal string
S → a S | b S | ε, which generates every string over {a,b} rather than the balanced ones
S → a b S | ε, which produces repetitions of the block ab instead of n a's then n b's
S → a S b | ab
questions.shortExplanation: Balanced a…b via S → aSb | ab.
questions.explanation: S → aSb | ab generates exactly equal numbers of a's then b's (n ≥ 1), capturing the nested structure regular expressions cannot.

questions.text: Why is left recursion harmless for bottom-up (LR) parsers but harmful for top-down parsers?
options: LR parsers expand nonterminals from the top, so they too loop forever on left recursion
Top-down parsers never use a stack and so cannot represent any recursion whatsoever
Left recursion silently changes the generated language whenever an LR parser processes it
LR parsers reduce handles bottom-up, consuming input before deciding the recursive rule
questions.shortExplanation: LR consumes input via shifts before reducing recursion.
questions.explanation: Bottom-up parsing shifts symbols and reduces handles, making progress on input, so left recursion does not loop; top-down expansion of a left-recursive rule loops without consuming input.

questions.text: A grammar in which every production has the form A → aB or A → a (a terminal, optional single trailing nonterminal) is:
options: Ambiguous by definition, since this restricted form always yields more than one parse tree
Right-linear, and therefore it generates a regular language accepted by a finite automaton
Always left-recursive, because the trailing nonterminal forces recursion on the left side
Context-sensitive, since a single trailing nonterminal exceeds the context-free restriction
questions.shortExplanation: Right-linear grammars generate regular languages.
questions.explanation: Right-linear (regular) grammars restrict productions so the recursion is at most a single trailing nonterminal, yielding exactly the regular languages.

questions.text: Substituting to remove a unit production A → B (where B → β₁ | β₂) results in:
options: A → B being retained unchanged, since unit productions cannot be removed without loss
Deleting the nonterminal A entirely from the grammar along with all of its productions
A → β₁ | β₂ added to replace the unit production, copying over the B's non-unit bodies
Adding a brand-new start symbol whose only purpose is to reference the nonterminal B
questions.shortExplanation: Replace A → B with B's right-hand sides.
questions.explanation: Unit-production removal copies each non-unit production of B directly into A, so A → B becomes A → β₁ | β₂, preserving the language.

questions.text: The MAIN reason syntax analysis uses context-free rather than context-sensitive grammars is that:
options: Context-sensitive grammars are inherently ambiguous and so cannot be parsed deterministically
Context-free parsing is efficient (often O(n)) while context-sensitive recognition is far more costly
Context-free grammars can fully express all of a language's type-checking and scope rules
Context-sensitive grammars are fundamentally incapable of describing programming languages
questions.shortExplanation: CFG parsing is efficient; CSG recognition is expensive.
questions.explanation: Context-free grammars admit efficient (often linear-time) parsers, whereas context-sensitive recognition is PSPACE -guess; context-sensitive checks (types) are deferred to semantic analysis.
